title: I Was Locked Inside a Supermarket After Closing. Then I Heard My Own Voice Coming From the Security Office (PART 2)

blocks.text: I didn't understand. I'd been at my father's funeral ten years ago. I'd stood in the front row and held my mother's hand.

The officer called the customer service manager, who'd been the one to accept the photograph. She'd gone home early, sick, and forgotten to tell the night staff. She picked up on the second ring. "Oh no," she said. "Is she there? Her name is Claire. She left a number."

Claire arrived twenty minutes later, breathless, in a green jacket exactly like mine. Up close, she was older than me, maybe thirty-four, but the resemblance was unsettling. Same eyes. Same chin. Same voice.
We sat on a bench by the bakery section with a police officer pretending not to listen.
Claire was my half-sister. Our father, a long-haul truck driver, had a relationship with her mother for a few years before he met mine.
He paid support but saw Claire only a handful of times. He told my mother about her. My mother never told me.

When our father died, Claire drove three hours to the funeral. My mother met her at the church door and asked her to leave, quietly, so I wouldn't find out. Claire left. She'd regretted it for ten years.

Last year, a DNA site matched us. She was too nervous to message me. She found my photography Instagram, saw that I shopped at this store on Thursday nights, and bought the same jacket so I'd notice her on camera if she ever got brave enough to approach me. She'd come in that afternoon to leave a photograph and a note with customer service, asking them to call her if I came in.
"I just didn't want you to walk past me forever."
I called my mother that night. She cried and admitted everything. She'd been afraid that if I knew about Claire, I'd think less of my father. She'd thought she was protecting his memory.

Claire and I have dinner every other week now. She tells me things about our father I never knew: he sang badly in the truck, he kept a photo of both of us on his dashboard. I tell her about the years she missed.
We still shop at that supermarket on Thursday nights. We just make sure to leave before closing.
